1	# kolosok-rehack — AI Development Guidelines
2	
3	Team **Kolosok** at the **European Hackathon League (EHL) Grand Finale**, Munich (TUM.ai).
4	This file is the rulebook for every AI agent (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, …) and human working in this repo.
5	**Read it fully before your first change.** Human setup (GitHub token, credentials) lives in `README-Human`.
6	
7	Source: [EHL Finale – All you need to know](https://tum-ai.notion.site/REDACTED)
8	
9	---
10	
11	## 0. Hard rules (non-negotiable)
12	
13	1. **Entire must be enabled and every commit must carry a checkpoint.** The organisers will reject a submission that does not use Entire. No Entire → no valid submission.
14	2. **All work goes through git and gets pushed to `origin`.** Nothing that exists only on one laptop counts.
15	3. **`main` must always be demo-able.** We have a strict 6-minute slot for pitch + demo + questions.
16	4. **Never commit secrets** (API keys, tokens, `.env`). Entire redacts secrets in session logs, but do not rely on that.
17	5. **Never rewrite pushed history** (no `push --force`, no amending/rebasing pushed commits, no deleting `entire/*` branches or refs). Checkpoints are tied to commits; rewriting history can orphan them.
18	
19	## 1. Key times (Munich local time)
20	
21	| When | What |
22	|---|---|
23	| Sat 10 Oct, 11:00–11:30 | Entire technical onboarding |
24	| **Sat 10 Oct, 13:00** | **Challenge selection deadline** (captain, on https://ehl.gg/) |
25	| Sat 13:30 → Sun 12:00 | Hacking |
26	| **Sun 11 Oct, 12:00** | **Submission deadline** — hard stop |
27	| Sun 12:00–14:30 | Challenge pitches (6 min incl. Q&A) |
28	| Sun 15:30–16:30 | Main-stage final (6 teams) |
29	
30	Internal targets: **feature freeze Sun 10:00**, first full submission by **Sun 10:30**, final re-submission by **11:45**.
31	Submissions can be repeated as often as we like before the deadline, so submit early and update.
32	
33	**Challenge:** BMW Group. _Brief details TBD; add a one-line summary of the task here._
34	
35	## 2. Setup checklist (each machine, once)
36	
37	Prerequisites: `git` on `PATH` (Entire shells out to it — it fails with `exec: "git": executable file not found` otherwise).
38	
39	```bash
40	# 1. Install Entire (bash / Git Bash). On Windows the binary ends up in ~/.local/bin/entire.exe
41	curl -fsSL https://entire.io/install.sh | bash
42	
43	# 2. On the main branch of this repo:
44	git checkout main && git pull
45	entire login                     # if not logged in yet
46	entire enable                    # enables session tracking in this repo
47	entire agent add claude-code     # install hooks for your agent; `entire agent list` shows others (codex, cursor, …)
48	
49	# 3. Verify
50	entire status
51	entire doctor                    # if anything looks off
52	```
53	
54	**You are set up correctly when** your next commit prints:
55	
56	```
57	[entire] Pushing 1 checkpoint ref(s) to origin.... done
58	```
59	
60	If you don't see that line, stop and fix Entire before writing more code.
61	
62	## 3. Git workflow
63	
64	- **Commit small and often** — at least every meaningful step, ideally every 15–30 min of agent work. Each commit becomes a checkpoint linking the code to the prompt/reasoning behind it.
65	- **Commit from within the agent session** (or right after it) so Entire attaches the session context to the commit.
66	- **Commit messages:** imperative, prefixed by area, e.g. `feat(api): add route planner endpoint`, `fix(ui): handle empty results`, `docs: update run instructions`. Types: `feat`, `fix`, `refactor`, `docs`, `chore`, `test`, `demo`.
67	- **Sync before push:** `git pull --rebase` on *unpushed* local commits only, then `git push`. Resolve conflicts, never discard teammates' work.
68	- **Branches:** short-lived feature branches (`feat/<topic>`, `fix/<topic>`) merged back to `main` quickly (within a few hours). Trivial fixes may go straight to `main`. Do not let branches drift overnight.
69	- **Do not commit:** `.env`, credentials, `node_modules/`, virtualenvs, large datasets or model weights, build artifacts. Add them to `.gitignore` as soon as they appear.
70	- **After every push** check the `[entire] Pushing … checkpoint ref(s)` line appeared.
71	
72	## 4. How agents should work here
73	
74	**Before starting a task**
75	1. Read this README and `README-Human`; look at `Concept/` for the architecture sketch (`root.drawio`).
76	2. `git pull` and check what others (human or agent) are doing:
77	   - `entire recap` — summary of recent checkpoint activity
78	   - `entire session list` — active/past agent sessions
79	   - `entire checkpoint search "<topic>"` — has someone already tried this?
80	3. Confirm the task is not already in progress to avoid duplicate work.
81	
82	**While working**
83	- Keep scope tight: do the requested task, nothing more. Hackathon time is the scarcest resource.
84	- Prefer simple, working solutions over clever ones; a reliable demo beats extra features.
85	- Match existing structure, naming, and style. Don't introduce new frameworks or languages without team agreement.
86	- Keep the app runnable at every commit. If you break `main`, fixing it is the top priority.
87	- Document how to run anything you add (see §6) in the same commit.
88	- Use `entire agent-help` for machine-readable, version-accurate CLI usage instead of guessing commands.
89	
90	**Handing off / resuming**
91	- Use `entire session resume <branch>` or `entire checkpoint explain <id|sha>` to pick up someone else's context instead of re-deriving it.
92	- `entire dispatch` produces a summary of recent agent work — use it for handoffs and pitch prep.
93	
94	**When unsure** about requirements or the challenge brief: ask the team; challenge questions go to the partners on **Discord** (https://discord.gg/4UDNd5TAg). Do not assume partner support is available overnight.
95	
96	## 5. LLMs, keys, and resources
97	
98	- **OpenAI** is a tech partner: each participant has **75 USD** of LLM/API credits. Use them for app-level LLM calls.
99	- Keys go in a local `.env` (gitignored) and are read via environment variables; provide a `.env.example` with placeholder names only.
100	- Be mindful of token spend; `entire session tokens <id>` / `entire checkpoint tokens <id>` show usage.
101	
102	## 6. Demo & submission readiness
103	
104	- Judging is a **strict 6-minute slot including questions** — design the product around one clear, rehearsable demo flow.
105	- Keep a **"How to run"** section here up to date (install, env vars, start command, demo script).
106	- Before submission: everything pushed, Entire checkpoints present (`entire checkpoint list`), all relevant content uploaded on https://ehl.gg/.
107	- Have a fallback (recorded video or screenshots) in case the live demo fails.
108	
109	### How to run
110	
111	_TBD — add install + start commands as soon as there is runnable code._
112	
113	## 7. Repo map
114	
115	| Path | Purpose |
116	|---|---|
117	| `README.md` | This file — AI/dev guidelines (agents: start here) |
118	| `CLAUDE.md`, `AGENTS.md` | Auto-loaded agent entry points; they point here |
119	| `README-Human` | Human onboarding: GitHub token & credential setup |
120	| `Concept/root.drawio` | Architecture / concept diagram |

Your mission
Build an AI-powered application that ingests heterogeneous data, derives customer requirements for a vehicle, prioritizes them, and puts a product manager in the loop at the decisions that matter.
Your app should be able to:
    Ingest the provided data and enrich it with structured knowledge from the web.
    Extract signals such as recurring complaints, unmet needs, competitor advantages and market trends, each linked to its sources.
    Derive requirements from those findings: clear, actionable, customer-facing and realistic.
    Prioritize them with a logic you define and can explain.
    Involve the PM to approve, reject, edit or challenge requirements and their rationale and evidence behind them. 
   Record everything in an audit trail (is a complete, chronological record of all actions, changes, and access events within a system or data environment).
About the Scope
In scope:
    Customer requirements on the product: features, equipment, comfort, space, usability, infotainment and digital services, design and quality perception, driving experience, range and charging as experienced by the customer, variant and package offering, etc.
Out of scope:
    Regulatory and homologation requirements (e.g.: safety, emissions, type approval)
    Technical and engineering requirements (e.g.: component specs, architecture, supplier topics)
   Pricing, business case and cost calculation (you may use cost or effort as a rough prioritization factor)
**Make it yours!**
Demonstrate your application at least for one derivative in onbe market but avoid designing it as a one-off: it should be adaptable to other BMW vehicles and markets. The remaining datasets and scenarios are available for optional testing. 
We know the challenge is broad. Focus on the parts where your team can make the strongest contribution. You might go deep on web research and turn external information into usable evidence, or on integrating and interpreting the provided BMW data. You do not need to develop every capability to the same depth. Be creative, but show how your chosen focus connects to the overall path from evidence to a PM decision.
**Expected Deliverables**
- A concept and demonstrable prototype of an AI-powered product requirements application that processes heterogeneous inputs, derives product requirements, supports prioritization, and integrates human review.
- A structured sample list of derived product requirements. Each requirement should include a unique identifier, a clear and actionable description, its linked findings and sources, a priority or score, the applied prioritization rationale, an evidence level, the key future-facing assumptions and uncertainties and its current decision status.
- A clearly defined end-to-end workflow showing how inputs are processed into proposed and prioritized requirements, which activities the AI performs autonomously, and where human review is mandatory. 
- A demonstrable audit trail that makes each requirement traceable from its underlying findings and sources through consolidation, scoring, prioritization, and human decision-making. It should record relevant changes to requirement content, scores, priorities, evidence, and status, including who or what initiated each change, when it occurred, and the documented rationale.
Important: Teams are free to choose their technical approach, architecture, prioritization logic, and user experience. The deliverables describe the capabilities and outcomes that should be demonstrated, not a prescribed solution design. Deliverables may be presented as one integrated solution or as a combination of connected concepts, prototypes, models, and visualizations.

# BMW Group Challenge — AI for Product Decision Making

Sources: `requirenments.pages` (main source, wins on any conflict), `BMW_Hackathon_Briefing_Short.pdf` (context and extras), `image.png` (data table).
Items marked _(PDF)_ come only from the PDF.

## The challenge

What should the next generation of a BMW vehicle offer its customers? Build an AI-powered application that helps product managers (PMs) derive, justify and prioritize **customer requirements** for a successor vehicle. Ground proposals in customer feedback, BMW product and sales data, and web research, while keeping the **PM firmly in control of every decision**. _(PDF)_

**Why it matters** _(PDF)_: Defining a new generation means understanding what customers value today and what they will value when the successor reaches the market. PM work today is manual, slow and hard to trace. AI should make evidence, assumptions and uncertainties transparent and under human control.

## Your mission

Build an AI-powered application that ingests heterogeneous data, derives customer requirements for a vehicle, prioritizes them, and puts a product manager in the loop at the decisions that matter.

The app should be able to:

1. **Ingest** the provided data and enrich it with structured knowledge from the web.
2. **Extract signals** such as recurring complaints, unmet needs, competitor advantages and market trends, each linked to its sources.
3. **Derive requirements** from those findings: clear, actionable, customer-facing and realistic.
4. **Prioritize** them with a logic you define and can explain.
5. **Involve the PM** to approve, reject, edit or challenge requirements and the rationale and evidence behind them.
6. **Record everything in an audit trail** (a complete, chronological record of all actions, changes and access events).

Extra context _(PDF)_:
- Use the BMW **1 Series, 5 Series, 7 Series**, or a combination.
- Focus on **Europe, China, the United States**, or any subset that best shows your approach.
- Think **3–5 years ahead**: which customer needs should shape the next generation?
- Make clear where conclusions rest on **evidence** and where on **forward-looking assumptions**.
- Judges care about how diverse information becomes actionable PM insight with transparent reasoning, not about a specific workflow or architecture.

## Scope

**In scope** — customer requirements on the product:
features, equipment, comfort, space, usability, infotainment and digital services, design and quality perception, driving experience, range and charging as experienced by the customer, variant and package offering, etc.

**Out of scope:**
- Regulatory and homologation requirements (safety, emissions, type approval)
- Technical and engineering requirements (component specs, architecture, supplier topics)
- Pricing, business case and cost calculation (cost or effort may be used as a rough prioritization factor)

## Data and sources

Provided data, per vehicle:

| Dataset | What it contains | What it is good for |
|---|---|---|
| Customer verbatims | Free-text customer feedback on the current vehicle | Pain points, unmet needs, what customers love and must not lose |
| Equipment list | Standard and optional equipment by trim and market | What the car offers today, gaps against competitors |
| Sales volumes | Units by powertrain and region | Where the car sells, which powertrains matter, where it underperforms |
| Customer study | Customer ratings in various categories | How customers perceive, like/dislike, rate different components of a car |

External enrichment is allowed _(PDF)_: competitor information, reviews, market and technology trends.

## Make it yours

- Demonstrate the app for **at least one derivative in one market**, but do not build it as a one-off: it should adapt to other BMW vehicles and markets. The remaining datasets and scenarios are available for optional testing.
- The challenge is broad. Focus where your team can contribute most (e.g. deep web research turned into usable evidence, or integrating and interpreting the BMW data). You do not need every capability at the same depth, but show how your focus connects the path **from evidence to a PM decision**.
- _(PDF)_ Valued: trustworthy sources, transparent reasoning, thoughtful prioritization, clear handling of uncertainty and conflicting evidence, and a view on how the concept scales across vehicle lines and markets.
- _(PDF)_ Focus on customer value, not engineering specs, regulation or detailed business cases.

## Expected deliverables

1. **Concept and demonstrable prototype** of an AI-powered product-requirements application that processes heterogeneous inputs, derives requirements, supports prioritization and integrates human review.
2. **Structured sample list of derived requirements.** Each requirement must include:
   - unique identifier
   - clear, actionable description
   - linked findings and sources
   - priority or score
   - applied prioritization rationale
   - evidence level
   - key future-facing assumptions and uncertainties
   - current decision status
3. **End-to-end workflow** showing how inputs become proposed and prioritized requirements, which steps the AI does autonomously, and where human review is **mandatory**.
4. **Demonstrable audit trail** making each requirement traceable from findings and sources, through consolidation, scoring, prioritization and the human decision. It must record changes to requirement content, scores, priorities, evidence and status, including **who or what** initiated each change, **when**, and the **documented rationale**.

**Important:** teams are free to choose technical approach, architecture, prioritization logic and UX. The deliverables describe capabilities and outcomes to demonstrate, not a prescribed design. They may be one integrated solution or a combination of connected concepts, prototypes, models and visualizations.

## What to demonstrate (short form) _(PDF)_

- A working prototype showing how AI supports identifying, formulating and prioritizing requirements from the provided data and external sources.
- A representative set of requirements with clear evidence and reasoning, showing which factors drive prioritization.
- A transparent decision-support experience where PMs can review, challenge, modify, approve or reject AI proposals, with evidence, assumptions, uncertainties and decisions visible and traceable throughout.

## Notes

- The Pages text said "at least for one derivative in onbe market"; read as "in one market".
- The Pages file did not list the 1/5/7 Series, regions or the 3–5 year horizon; those come from the PDF.

Pushed (`3834611` on `main`). It carries `Entire-Checkpoint: 01M4K2JE8MRM75B1XDGMRPK3P0`, and the checkpoint refs are on the remote.

The first push was rejected because a teammate had pushed first. I ran `git pull --rebase` and pushed again, which is the README's own rule for unpushed commits. Your README edits (the `pull.rebase` line and the checkpoint check) came in with that pull.

## Does the README make sense?

Yes. It's consistent and the rules don't contradict each other. A few things are worth a look:

1. **`README-Human` is Windows-only.** Step 3 uses PowerShell and Windows Credential Manager, but your machine is a Mac. If a push asks for a password again, the Mac equivalent is `git credential-osxkeychain erase`. Also, the file opens with `'''` markers, which look like a leftover.
2. **There's no `.gitignore` inside the repo.** The README says to add one as soon as build files appear, so add it before the first real code. Your `.env` lives one folder up, outside the repo, so that's safe for now.
3. **The key-times table is partly stale.** The challenge-selection deadline (Sat 13:00) has passed and BMW is chosen. This is harmless, but you could mark it done.
4. **"How to run" is still TBD.** That's fine for now, but judges and teammates need it filled in once there's code. It's the main gap before submission.
5. **The README is a rulebook, not a project plan.** It says nothing about what you're building. Now that `BMW-Challenge.md` exists, the next useful step is a short "our approach" section, or a look at `Concept/root.drawio`.
6. **Mind the "no checkpoint" cases.** Commits made by hand, merge commits, and edits through shell commands get no checkpoint. After any `git pull` that creates a merge commit, check `git log -1 --format=%B`. Your `pull.rebase true` line prevents most of this.

One thing I didn't check is whether `.idea/` is committed or ignored. It's probably editor settings that shouldn't be in the repo, and it's quick to check with `git ls-files .idea`.
